title: Can Venus Cast a Shadow? Here's How to See It for Yourself
summary:
Have you ever heard that Venus can cast a shadow? It sounds like a myth, but it's actually true! Venus is the third-brightest object in our sky, after the sun and the moon. When it's at its brightest, it can make a faint shadow. But you can't see it in a city with all the lights. You need a really dark, clear sky.

Right now, Venus is getting brighter in the evening sky. It reached its 'half-lit' phase on August 12, and now it's becoming a crescent as it gets closer to Earth. That makes it shine even brighter! On August 14-15, it will be about 46 degrees from the sun and shine at magnitude -4.3 to -4.4. That's bright enough to see easily after sunset.

The best time to try to see Venus's shadow is around September 18, when it reaches its greatest brilliancy at magnitude -4.6. But from some places, it will be low in the sky, so you might need to find a good spot.

Here's how to see it: Find a dark place away from lights. Wait until twilight is over. Face Venus and put a white card or sheet on the ground, also facing Venus. Then put something in front of the card to cast a shadow, like a pencil or your hand. You might need to take a photo with a long exposure to see it clearly.

If you can't see the shadow, try another cool trick: photograph Venus's light reflecting on water! Any pond, lake, or ocean between you and Venus will catch its shine in a long exposure.

This is a great week for stargazing. There's a new moon, so the sky is dark. You might also see the crescent moon near Venus on August 15 or 16, and look for 'earthshine' on the moon's dark part. And don't forget the Milky Way, which is visible in dark skies this month. So grab a camera and head outside—the universe is full of wonders!
why_it_matters: Stargazing shows that you can discover amazing things with simple tools, a dark sky, and patience, even without a telescope or a science lab.

questions.question: What can you look for on the moon's dark part?

background_read: Venus is the second planet from the sun and is often called the brightest planet in Earth's sky because its thick clouds reflect lots of sunlight.
Planets do not make their own light; they shine by reflecting sunlight, just like the moon does.
Earthshine is sunlight bouncing off Earth onto the moon, and it can make the moon's dark part glow faintly.
Article_Structure: WHO: Stargazers who want to see a rare sight: Venus casting a shadow.
WHAT: Venus is bright enough to cast a faint shadow, and right now it is getting brighter as a crescent in the evening sky.
WHERE: You need a dark place away from city lights, with a white card or sheet on the ground facing Venus.
WHY: The best chance comes around September 18, when Venus reaches its greatest brilliancy, though it may sit low in the sky.

perspectives.description: They are excited to try the white-card trick and photograph Venus's faint shadow for themselves.
They may feel frustrated because bright lights and buildings can hide faint sky sights like Venus's shadow.
They know that dark skies, long camera exposures, and reflected light on water can reveal things eyes alone often miss.
